summary:
Project Orbit is a browser game for one to four players. Each player takes one role in a mission team: flight, science, power or communications. The team picks a scenario (orbit, landing or exploration) and a real mission target, such as Mercury, the Moon or a comet. Then the team designs the spacecraft from real parts, selects a rocket from the NASA catalog, plans the route and prepares contingency plans. Every choice changes mass, power, data, cost and risk. A mission clock counts in months. NASA data (POWER, JPL Horizons and OMNI2) sets bad launch months, solar storms and other events. Investors can add to the budget or cut it. After a GO/NO-GO vote, the game simulates the mission phase by phase. The final report explains each failure: the cause, the decision and what would have prevented it.

The game meets the challenge directly. Players design, manage and simulate a complete mission with limited resources, and they see how each decision affects success. The game gives hints from physical data, not answers. When no public data exists for a value, the game shows a cited equation and marks the value as an estimate. Project Orbit matters because it teaches the real trade-offs of mission design through teamwork. It runs in English and Spanish, and it needs no installation.
details:
Project Details

What it does

Project Orbit is a multiplayer mission design game that runs in a web browser. One to four players sit in a shared 3D briefing room. Each player has one department, and each department matches a segment of a NASA science mission:

  • Flight is the launch segment (rocket and route).
  • Power is the space segment (solar panels, batteries, thermal control).
  • Communications is the ground segment (antennas and data link).
  • Science is the user segment (instruments and objectives).

How it works

  1. The team selects a scenario (orbit, landing or exploration) and a mission, for example a Mercury orbiter, a lunar lander or a comet probe.
  2. Each player builds their part of the spacecraft on a laptop in the 3D room. The parts have real mass, power, volume, data rate and price.
  3. Six shared bars show mass, power, battery, data, budget and volume. A design can exceed a limit by 20 % at most.
  4. On the wall of the control room, Flight plans the route and the launch window. The site maps come from LROC, LOLA, MESSENGER and OSIRIS-REx data.
  5. A mission clock counts in months from 2027 to 2031. Climate data from NASA POWER sets the weather risk at the launch site for each month. JPL Horizons sets the geometry of each target body, and DONKI sets the space weather risk. Events and investors change the budget and the schedule, so the best plan can change while the team works.
  6. Each department votes GO or NO-GO. Then the game flies the mission phase by phase, with a two-body orbit propagator (RK4) and live telemetry. The department that owns a contingency activates it when a problem occurs.
  7. The flight report shows each failure, the decision that caused it and how to prevent it next time. It also compares the design with the real mission it resembles, such as BepiColombo, Rosetta or Blue Ghost.

Benefits and intended impact

Real mission design is teamwork. One subsystem cannot change without an effect on the others. Players learn this through play, not from a lecture: a bigger antenna costs mass, more mass needs a bigger rocket, and a bigger rocket uses budget that science needs. We want students and the public to understand why missions take years and cost so much. We also want them to see why some missions fail. The game is free, needs no installation, and runs in English and Spanish, so it can reach classrooms in Latin America and in other places.

Tools and technologies

  • JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS, with no build step
  • Three.js 0.180 for the low-poly 3D rooms
  • mqtt.js 5.16.1 over several public MQTT brokers for multiplayer, with no game server
  • GitHub Pages for hosting
  • Python scripts to prepare NASA data (POWER, Horizons, OMNI2) and pixel font accents
  • An in-browser test suite for the network protocol and the game rules
  • Claude Code as an assistant for research, code and review

Creativity

  • A game of discussion. Most space games give one player full control of a rocket or a spacecraft. Project Orbit gives each player only one department and only part of the information. No player can win alone. The team must talk, negotiate and agree, the way a real mission team does in a design review.
  • Conflicts are part of the design. The goals of the departments compete. Science wants more instruments, Power wants a lighter spacecraft, Communications wants a bigger antenna, and Flight must keep everything inside the rocket and the budget. Each trade-off becomes a conversation, and each team finds its own compromise.
  • Many possible missions. The game has no single correct solution. Different combinations of parts, rockets, routes, launch months and contingency plans give different results. Events and investors also change the conditions during play. Two teams with the same mission can tell two very different stories, and the same team can play again and try a new strategy.
  • Shared responsibility. Before launch, each department must vote GO or NO-GO. After the flight, the report shows which decision caused each problem. This makes the team discuss what went wrong and plan a better mission.
  • A room for discussion. The game happens in one shared 3D space. The interfaces appear on objects in the room: laptops, a projector, folders on the table and the wall of a mission control room. Players see each other’s seats and where each player looks, so the discussion feels like a meeting around one table.
  • Hints, not answers. The game shows physical data and units, not the best choice. The team must interpret the data together, and this gives them more to discuss.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific honesty: each value has a source and a confidence level, and the game marks the estimates.
  • Access: a browser game that works on a normal laptop, in two languages, with a solo mode for players who have no team.
  • Network limits: no private server, and the game sends the messages through several redundant brokers.
  • Learning: the failure report explains causes and does not only give a score.
  • Scope: one complete, playable mission path in the time of the hackathon, with data ready to add more missions.
